title: Dynamic programming in Java (int[] tables, overflow, recursion depth)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Coin change, LCS and knapsack with int[] tables, overflow-safe sentinels, long counts, boxing in memo maps and recursion depth limits.
source: Oracle Java language specification (integer overflow); CLRS ch. 14-15; LeetCode Coin Change, Longest Common Subsequence; GeeksforGeeks 0/1 knapsack

questions.prompt: Using an int[] dp with dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2], dp[0] = 0, dp[1] = 1, what is the smallest i for which the true Fibonacci number no longer fits in a Java int (above 2,147,483,647)?
questions.explanation: fib(46) = 1,836,311,903 still fits, but fib(47) = 2,971,215,073 exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE and the int silently wraps to a negative value. Use long (good to fib(92)) or BigInteger.

questions.prompt: For "kitten" and "sitting", the Java edit distance table is allocated as new int[7][8]. How many cells does it contain?
questions.explanation: (m + 1) x (n + 1) = 7 x 8 = 56 cells, which include the empty-prefix row and column. Time and space are both proportional to this count.

questions.prompt: You count monotone paths in a 20 x 20 grid, moving only right or down. The answer is C(38, 19), about 35 billion. Which element type should the dp table use?
questions.explanation: Counting DPs overflow quickly. Mention the modulus (often 10^9 + 7) or long/BigInteger as soon as counts can be large.

options.text: long[][], because the count exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE.
options.why: Correct: 35 billion needs 64 bits, so int would wrap silently.

options.text: int[][], because Java int is large enough for any array index.
options.why: An index is small, but the values stored can be far larger than an int.

options.text: float[][], which holds values this large without wrapping.
options.why: float loses exact integer precision above 2^24, corrupting the counts.

options.text: byte[][], to save memory, since each cell adds only two terms.
options.why: Each term grows combinatorially; a byte overflows after 127.

questions.prompt: A memoised recursive coinChange(amount) works for amount = 1000 but throws StackOverflowError for amount = 100000. What is the most robust fix?
questions.explanation: Running the work in a Thread with a larger stack size also works, but tabulation is the interview answer. Recursion depth equals the longest chain of sub-amounts.

options.text: Switch to a bottom-up int[] table, which needs no deep call stack.
options.why: Correct: a loop fills the table in order, with constant stack usage.

options.text: Catch the StackOverflowError and retry with the same recursive method.
options.why: The retry hits the same depth limit, so it fails again.

options.text: Replace the int[] memo with a HashMap so the recursion is shallower.
options.why: The container does not change how deep the recursion goes.

options.text: Declare the recursive method synchronized to enlarge its stack frame.
options.why: synchronized adds locking and does nothing for stack depth.

questions.prompt: True or false: in a memo array created with new int[n + 1], using 0 to mean 'not computed yet' is safe even when some states legitimately have the value 0.
questions.explanation: Collisions with the sentinel do not break correctness but destroy the complexity bound, turning memoisation back into brute force.

options.why: A legitimate 0 would be mistaken for 'not computed' and recomputed every time.
Correct: Java zero-fills new int arrays, so 0 collides with real zero results; use -1 via Arrays.fill, or an Integer[] with null.

questions.prompt: A coin change solution fills dp with Integer.MAX_VALUE as 'impossible' and computes dp[a - c] + 1 without checking.
questions.explanation: Use amount + 1 as infinity, or skip unreachable sub-amounts before adding.
questions.assertion: Using Integer.MAX_VALUE as the 'impossible' marker can corrupt the table.
questions.reason: Adding 1 to Integer.MAX_VALUE wraps around to Integer.MIN_VALUE.

whys.a: Right: the wrapped value is hugely negative, so Math.min picks it as the best answer.
whys.b: R is the direct cause of A.

questions.prompt: A Java DP table is declared as int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1].
questions.explanation: Because rows are separate objects, you can swap two row references in O(1), the basis of rolling-row optimisation.
questions.assertion: The statement allocates a rectangular table of (m + 1) x (n + 1) cells.
questions.reason: A Java 2D array is an array whose elements are references to row arrays.

whys.a: The array-of-arrays layout does not by itself make the table rectangular; the sizes passed do.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but the rectangular shape comes from the two sizes given, not from the layout.

questions.prompt: In the single-array 0/1 knapsack the capacity loop runs from cap down to wt[i].
questions.explanation: Going downward means dp[w - wt] has not yet been updated for the current item.
questions.assertion: Running the capacity loop downward is required so that each item is used at most once.
questions.reason: Java copies an array on assignment, so dp keeps the previous item's row.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but Java assignment of an array copies only the reference, so R is false; the downward order is what preserves old values.

questions.prompt: Memoising a dense DP with a HashMap<Integer, Integer> instead of an int[].
questions.explanation: Use int[] (or long[]) when states are dense small integers; a map only pays off for sparse states.
questions.assertion: The HashMap version is faster than an int[] memo for dense state spaces.
questions.reason: Each put and get on a HashMap<Integer, Integer> boxes ints into Integer objects.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: R is true, and the boxing plus hashing cost is exactly why the map is slower, so A is false.
